title: Architecting Sub-150ms Hybrid RAG for Voice Agents: Combining pgvector, BM25, and Async FastAPI
excerpt: How we serve a 1,881-SKU industrial catalog over a voice channel without blowing the 700ms response budget and why a single Postgres instance beat the dedicated vector database we almost adopted.
body:
Architecting Sub-150ms Hybrid RAG for Voice Agents: Combining pgvector, BM25, and Async FastAPI Event Loops

How we serve a 1,881-SKU industrial catalog over a voice channel without blowing the 700ms response budget and why a single Postgres instance beat the dedicated vector database we almost adopted.

The Phone Call That Killed Our Original Stack

A customer asked our voice agent for “the 9921X.” Pause. Then: “the SKU-9921X, in the bronze finish.”

Our pgvector-only retriever returned five semantically related parts. None of them were SKU-9921X. The agent confidently described an adjacent product. The customer hung up.

I pulled the trace. The query embedding from text-embedding-3-small had collapsed the string “SKU-9921X” into roughly the same neighborhood as “industrial part,” “inventory item,” and “stock query.” Dense embeddings, trained to capture conceptual meaning, treat alphanumeric identifiers as near-meaningless token salad. The model isn’t broken — it’s working exactly as designed. It just wasn’t designed for catalog lookup.

That was the moment we stopped pretending vector search alone was a retrieval strategy.

What follows is the architecture we shipped after that incident: a hybrid retrieval pipeline running in one Postgres instance, fused by Reciprocal Rank Fusion, reranked locally on a single GPU, orchestrated by an async event loop that lives or dies by tail latency. p50 for the full RAG window — embedding to top-5 documents — sits at 101ms. p99 is 138ms. The pipeline holds inside a 150ms budget, with 49ms of headroom we use for circuit-breaker fallbacks.

This is a story about milliseconds, the math of rank fusion, and why “use a real vector database” is, at 1,881 documents, the wrong instinct.

Pillar 1: Where the Milliseconds Actually Go

The 150ms figure is meaningless without the surrounding budget. Voice agents have one perception threshold that matters: the gap between the user finishing a sentence and the agent beginning to speak. Cross 800ms and the interaction feels broken. Stay under 600ms and it feels human. Our target sits at 700ms comfortably human, with margin for the bad p99 days.

Here is the actual budget, measured on our production pipeline:

Stagep50p99NotesSTT end-of-speech → final transcript (Deepgram Nova-3, streaming)220ms310msVendor-controlled. We don’t own this.Hybrid RAG window (search + rerank, our scope)101ms138msThe subject of this article.LLM TTFT (Groq Llama-3.3–70B-Versatile, streaming)180ms240msVendor-controlled, but model choice matters.TTS first audio chunk (ElevenLabs Flash v2.5)110ms165msVendor-controlled.Async orchestration + network jitter50ms120msThis is where most teams bleed time without noticing.End-to-end (perceived)661ms973msThe p99 violation is almost always orchestration, not models.

Two observations shaped everything else.

First: the RAG window is the only stage we control. STT, LLM, and TTS are external services with fixed-cost latency floors. We picked Groq for the LLM precisely because Anthropic and OpenAI’s lower-latency tiers still add 250–400ms of TTFT, enough to push us past 800ms. The choice of LLM provider is a latency decision before it’s a quality decision.

Second: the orchestration overhead is bigger than the entire retrieval pipeline. If you take one thing from this article, take that. Most engineers I talk to spend weeks tuning HNSW parameters and zero hours on connection pool warmup, DNS caching, and asyncio.gather ordering. That ratio is backwards.

Pillar 2: Why One Postgres Instance Beats Pinecone, Weaviate, and Qdrant

We benchmarked all three. Then we kept Postgres.

At 1,881 documents and even at the 50,000 we project for next year , a managed vector database adds a network hop, an auth handshake, and a separate consistency surface in exchange for index quality you don’t need at this scale. The pgvector HNSW implementation is honestly very close to the dedicated engines for any catalog under a million vectors. The latency you save on the engine is dwarfed by the latency you spend reaching it.

More importantly, hybrid retrieval in two systems forces you to either run two queries in parallel and merge in application code, or pre-compute fusion at index time. Both approaches make your tail latency worse and your operational story messier. In Postgres, the dense and sparse retrievals are one query, one transaction, one network round-trip.

Our schema, simplified:

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS unaccent;
CREATE TABLE products (
    id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    sku             TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
    title           TEXT NOT NULL,
    description     TEXT NOT NULL,
    embedding       VECTOR(1536) NOT NULL,
    search_vector   TSVECTOR GENERATED ALWAYS AS (
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', unaccent(sku)),         'A') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', unaccent(title)),       'B') ||
        setweight(to_tsvector('english', unaccent(description)), 'C')
    ) STORED
);
CREATE INDEX products_embedding_hnsw
    ON products USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
    WITH (m = 16, ef_construction = 64);
CREATE INDEX products_search_gin
    ON products USING gin (search_vector);

The setweight call is the part most tutorials skip. The SKU field is weighted “A” (highest), the title “B”, and the description “C”. This means an exact SKU match dominates the lexical score even when the description contains many query terms. That single design decision is why “SKU-9921X” now returns SKU-9921X.

One precision note for the careful reader: the title of this article says BM25 because that’s the term the industry uses for sparse lexical retrieval. Postgres ts_rank_cd is technically BM25-flavored cover-density ranking, not strict Okapi BM25. For our use case, the difference is academic — for yours, it might not be. If you need true BM25 inside Postgres, look at the VectorChord-bm25 extension, which TensorChord released in 2025.

Pillar 3: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, the Math That Made It Work

Combining a dense score and a sparse score into a single ranked list sounds easy until you try it. Cosine distance is bounded [0, 2]. ts_rank_cd is unbounded and corpus-dependent. Min-max normalization is fragile to outliers. Z-score normalization assumes a distribution your scores don’t actually follow.

Reciprocal Rank Fusion sidesteps all of that. You throw away the scores entirely and keep only the ranks.

RRF(d) = \sum_{r \in R} \frac{1}{k + r(d)}

Where RRR is the set of ranking systems (in our case: dense and sparse), r(d)r(d)r(d) is the rank of document ddd in that ranking, and kkk is a smoothing constant. The standard k=60k = 60k=60 from the original Cormack et al. paper has held up across a decade of benchmarking papers. We tested 30, 60, and 100. The differences in nDCG@5 were inside noise. We kept 60.

The elegance of RRF is that it requires no normalization, no training, and no per-corpus tuning. A document that ranks #1 in dense and #1 in sparse gets a score of:


\frac{1}{61} + \frac{1}{61} \approx 0.0328

A document that ranks #1 in dense but doesn't appear in sparse at all gets:


\frac{1}{61} \approx 0.0164

A document at rank #50 in both gets:

\frac{2}{110} \approx 0.0182

The math naturally rewards documents that appear high in both lists, which is exactly the signal hybrid retrieval is supposed to surface.

Implemented as a single SQL statement against the schema above:

WITH dense AS (
    SELECT id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY embedding <=> $1) AS rank
    FROM products
    ORDER BY embedding <=> $1
    LIMIT 50
),
sparse AS (
    SELECT id,
           ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(search_vector, q) DESC) AS rank
    FROM products, websearch_to_tsquery('english', unaccent($2)) AS q
    WHERE search_vector @@ q
    ORDER BY ts_rank_cd(search_vector, q) DESC
    LIMIT 50
)
SELECT COALESCE(d.id, s.id) AS id,
       (COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + d.rank), 0)
      + COALESCE(1.0 / (60 + s.rank), 0)) AS rrf_score
FROM dense d
FULL OUTER JOIN sparse s ON d.id = s.id
ORDER BY rrf_score DESC
LIMIT 50;

The FULL OUTER JOIN matters. A document that appears in only one ranking still gets through with half the maximum possible RRF score. Use an inner join and you silently drop everything that fired on one retriever and not the other , which is most of the long tail.

p50 for this query against our 1,881-row table with both indexes warm: 8.3ms.

Pillar 4: The Async Pipeline (the Actual Code We Run)

Two principles drive the orchestration code.

First: any operation that can run in parallel with the database round-trip must. The query embedding call to OpenAI and the connection acquisition from asyncpg’s pool both take real time. Doing them sequentially is throwing away 30–40ms for nothing.

Second: the reranker has a hard ceiling. If it doesn’t return in 80ms, we ship the raw RRF order and move on. Conversational latency is non-negotiable; reranker quality is.

import asyncio
import asyncpg
from dataclasses import dataclass
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from sentence_transformers import CrossEncoder
HYBRID_SQL = """ -- the query from the previous section, loaded once at boot """@dataclass(slots=True)
class Candidate:
    id: int
    rrf_score: floatclass HybridRetriever:
    def __init__(
        self,
        pool: asyncpg.Pool,
        openai: AsyncOpenAI,
        reranker: CrossEncoder,
        rerank_timeout_s: float = 0.080,
        gpu_concurrency: int = 4,
    ):
        self.pool = pool
        self.openai = openai
        self.reranker = reranker
        self.rerank_timeout_s = rerank_timeout_s
        # Bound the number of concurrent reranker calls so a burst of voice
        # turns can't queue past the GPU's batch capacity.
        self._gpu = asyncio.Semaphore(gpu_concurrency)async def _embed(self, text: str) -> list[float]:
        resp = await self.openai.embeddings.create(
            model="text-embedding-3-small",
            input=text,
            dimensions=1536,
        )
        return resp.data[0].embeddingasync def retrieve(self, query: str, k: int = 5) -> list[Candidate]:
        # Overlap the embedding HTTP call with pool acquisition.
        # On a warm pool this saves 8-12ms. On a cold pool it saves 40ms+.
        emb_task = asyncio.create_task(self._embed(query))
        conn_task = asyncio.create_task(self.pool.acquire())try:
            embedding, conn = await asyncio.gather(emb_task, conn_task)
        except BaseException:
            emb_task.cancel()
            conn_task.cancel()
            raisetry:
            rows = await conn.fetch(HYBRID_SQL, embedding, query)
        finally:
            await self.pool.release(conn)candidates = [Candidate(id=r["id"], rrf_score=r["rrf_score"]) for r in rows]# Circuit breaker: if rerank takes more than 80ms, fall back to RRF.
        # Below the GPU is also gated by a semaphore so we don't thundering-herd it.
        try:
            async with asyncio.timeout(self.rerank_timeout_s):
                async with self._gpu:
                    return await self._rerank(query, candidates, k)
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            return candidates[:k]async def _rerank(
        self, query: str, candidates: list[Candidate], k: int
    ) -> list[Candidate]:
        # CrossEncoder.predict is blocking — push it off the event loop.
        loop = asyncio.get_running_loop()
        # Caller owns hydration of (title, description) — kept off the hot path.
        pairs = [(query, c.text_for_rerank) for c in candidates]
        scores = await loop.run_in_executor(None, self.reranker.predict, pairs)
        ranked = sorted(
            zip(candidates, scores, strict=True),
            key=lambda pair: pair[1],
            reverse=True,
        )
        return [c for c, _ in ranked[:k]]

Things in this code that are not obvious:

  • asyncio.timeout (Python 3.11+) is structured concurrency — it cancels the inner task cleanly when the budget runs out. Pre-3.11 wait_for works, but its cancellation semantics are messier and leak more often.
  • The gpu_concurrency semaphore is not optional. Without it, a momentary spike of concurrent voice turns saturates the GPU’s internal batching window and every request goes into a queue. p99 doubles. We learned this in staging at 50 RPS.
  • pool.release lives in a finally block because if the gather raises mid-flight, the connection still has to come back to the pool. asyncpg will not reclaim it for you.
  • run_in_executor is there because CrossEncoder.predict is blocking CPU/GPU work. Calling it directly on the event loop blocks every other coroutine. This is the single most common mistake I see in async RAG code.

The Reranker Trade-off: Cloud Latency Is a Lie

Our first reranker was Cohere rerank-3. The API is excellent. The model is excellent. The latency numbers Cohere publishes are excellent.

In production, we measured p50 at 90ms and p99 at 810ms.

The p99 is not the model’s fault. It’s cross-region routing, TLS renegotiation, occasional rate-limit handshakes, and the simple physics of a network call to someone else’s data center. None of that is fixable from our side. And in a voice agent, a single 800ms tail blows the entire response budget — the user hears a noticeable pause, registers it as broken, and either repeats the question (now you have two requests in flight) or hangs up.

We moved to bge-reranker-base running locally on a single AWS g6.xlarge instance — one NVIDIA L4 GPU, 24GB, $0.83 per hour. The model loads at boot, lives in VRAM, and accepts batches of up to 32 query-document pairs. Quality is comparable to Cohere’s smaller models on our domain; we ran a 500-query labeled evaluation and the nDCG@5 difference was 0.013, well inside noise.

Latency numbers on that instance, measured over 30 days of production traffic:

  • p50: 47ms (50 candidates, batched, FP16)
  • p95: 71ms
  • p99: 95ms
  • Timeout rate (>80ms, falls back to RRF): 0.3%

The 0.3% fallback rate is acceptable because RRF on a 50-candidate hybrid pool is already a strong baseline. We pulled a sample of 200 timed-out requests and rated retrieval quality by hand. The RRF-only top-5 was equivalent or better than the reranker top-5 in 71% of cases. The reranker is a quality boost, not a correctness layer. Build accordingly.

What’s Still Hard

If this all sounds clean, I am understating the chaos.

The L4 is a single point of failure. We have a hot standby with the model pre-loaded, but failover is manual and takes about 90 seconds. Multi-region active-active is on the roadmap and is not free.

Multilingual is barely working. The english tsvector config is wrong for our Spanish-speaking customers, and pgvector’s distance metric doesn’t care about the embedding model’s per-language quality drift. We’re piloting per-language partial indexes and a Cohere multilingual embedding model in a separate column. Not solved.

The 700ms budget assumes a healthy AWS us-east-1. We’ve eaten 1.5-second response times when a single AZ degrades. The right answer is probably edge STT and edge TTS providers, but the engineering cost is real and we haven’t paid it yet.

And the catalog will grow. At 50,000 SKUs, the HNSW recall starts to droop without bigger ef_search, which trades latency for quality. At 500,000 SKUs, the math changes and a dedicated engine starts winning again. Architecture decisions have an expiration date. Ours is probably 18 months.

What Actually Generalizes

If you’re building voice RAG, three takeaways from our two years on this stack:

  1. Hybrid retrieval is not optional for any catalog containing identifiers, model numbers, or codes. Dense embeddings will silently fail on them, and your evaluations won’t catch it unless you specifically test for it.
  2. Postgres is the right answer until it isn’t. Run the numbers for your scale. Most teams adopt dedicated vector databases ~10× earlier than they need to and pay for the privilege in operational complexity.
  3. Tail latency is the budget. A p50 win that comes with p99 regression is a loss. Reranker circuit breakers, connection pool warmup, and asyncio orchestration matter more than HNSW tuning at the scales most production systems actually run at.
